title: The Tamiḻ Concept of Love
paragraphs: > Look at the commentary of the passionate Tamiḻ scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar > On the Tolkāppiyam verse on the nature of clandestine love! > We will understand > Why Tolkāppiyar refers here to the eight kinds of marriage in the Aryan land. > > These kinds stand flawed, > Unacceptable to the impeccable Tamiḻ mind; > They might suit only the Aryan culture > In their entirety; > And just one or two of them correspond to the Tamiḻ ethos - > So says the learned Tamiḻ commentator. > > What then are those eight kinds of marriage? > Piramam is gifting a girl of twelve > To a bachelor nearing fifty years of age; > Giving a girl in marriage to the brother-in-law by relation > With the mutual parental consent

> Is what is called piracāpattiyam; > Āriṭam is taking a girl in marriage > Along with the gift of cattle; > Giving the girl’s hand to a performer of sacrifice > Before the sacrificial fire is teyvam; > Gandharvam is the union of love > Between a man and a woman running into each other; > Acuram is giving the girl learned to one adept in archery > Who tames a killer bull > And who is after gifts of wealth; > Irākkatam is coercive marriage of a girl by a boy: > And paicācam is union with a girl > Older by age, given to sleep and drink. > > Tolkāppiyar identifies these forms > As those of the Vedic Aryan culture > And rejects them subtly > And they do not go with the Tamiḻ mores, > So says our respected Tamiḻ scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar. > > Kaḷavu is theft, stealing small things; > It is quite natural that it is despised as an act of wrong kind. > > But kaḷavu as a union of love -- > Between a man and a woman > Who are united by the union of hearts > With no hurry for physical intimacy, > Who do not transgress the bounds of propriety > And who meet clandestinely > Aided by their kindly companions, > Whose bond of union courses through > Ways of virtue and love > Combined with codes of worldly needs > The bond uniting the two as one
> That comes in for acclaim > In Tamiḻ > Sweet as the strain of the lute > And the deep-sea pearl -- > Is no thing of a lowly worth > Even to men of lowly birth.

> Examined rightly, > The union of love between a man and a woman, > Which embraces the fivefold love behaviour mutually realized, > (Union, forbearance, separation, sulking and lamentation) > And which draws on the pleasures of love, life’s plenty and righteousness, > Shares the nature of the love of the gandharvas adept at lyre play > Which is among the eight forms of marriage vogue among the vedic folk. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 1)

Note: Tolkāppiyar had to make a reference to the vedic forms of marriage and contrast them with those of the Tamiḻ culture, for during his time, the vedic culture started taking roots on the Tamiḻ soil. The eight kinds of vedic marriage contrast with the three kinds treated in Tolkāppiyam, namely: mutual love (aṉpiṉ aintiṇai), one-sided love (kaikkiḷai) and abnormal sexual passion (peruntiṇai).
